questions.q: In msdb.dbo.backupset, what does a type value of 'D' represent?
options: A full database backup
A differential backup
A transaction log backup
A failed backup attempt
questions.explain: backupset.type uses 'D' for a full database backup, 'I' for differential, and 'L' for a transaction log backup.

questions.q: Why does the backup status section use a LEFT JOIN from sys.databases to msdb.dbo.backupset instead of an inner join?
options: So a database that has never been backed up still appears in the results, flagged as NEVER BACKED UP, instead of being silently dropped
LEFT JOIN runs faster than INNER JOIN in every case
backupset requires a LEFT JOIN by SQL Server syntax rules
It has no effect on the results either way
questions.explain: An inner join would omit any database with zero matching backupset rows. A LEFT JOIN keeps it in the result set with NULL backup dates, which the CASE expression turns into a NEVER BACKED UP flag.

questions.q: Why is the failed-jobs section in this lesson bounded by @JobLookbackHours, unlike Lesson 29's original query?
options: So the morning check only surfaces recent failures instead of every failure in sysjobhistory's entire retention window
Because sysjobhistory only stores 24 hours of data by default
Because msdb.dbo.agent_datetime requires a bounded range to run at all
It has no practical effect on the query's output
questions.explain: A morning check should focus on last night's failures, not the entire history retained in sysjobhistory. The lookback window keeps the output relevant to what needs a response today.

questions.q: What does the full_backup_status column's OVERDUE value indicate?
options: The most recent full backup's finish date is further in the past than @FullBackupThresholdHours allows
The backup job failed with an error
The database is in SIMPLE recovery model
The backup file could not be found on disk
questions.explain: OVERDUE is computed purely from timing: DATEDIFF(HOUR, last full backup, GETDATE()) exceeding the threshold, regardless of whether any job reported an error.

questions.q: Why does the failed-jobs query filter on h.step_id <> 0 in addition to h.run_status = 0?
options: Because the step_id = 0 row is only a summary row, and the actual failing step with its error message lives in the step-level rows
Because step_id 0 always represents a successful run
Because sysjobhistory does not allow querying step_id 0 directly
It has no effect — step_id 0 rows never have run_status = 0
questions.explain: step_id = 0 is a job-level summary row. Filtering it out and keeping step_id <> 0 surfaces the specific step that failed, along with its message.
